items.prompt: Define recruitment.
items.canonical_answer: Recruitment is the process of identifying that the business needs a new employee and attracting suitable people to apply for the vacancy. Internal recruitment fills the vacancy with a candidate who already works for the business; external recruitment attracts candidates from outside it.

items.prompt: Explain how a business benefits from using a practical test, such as a typing test, when selecting a receptionist.
items.canonical_answer: A practical test gathers evidence of the skill the job actually needs, which a conversation alone cannot, so the business is more likely to appoint someone who can genuinely do the work. Because the appointee can do the work, fewer mistakes reach customers, which leads to fewer complaints and less time spent correcting errors - so the benefit develops from better appointment to better service.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the test gathering checkable evidence about job-relevant skill, because the business can see the candidate doing the work, developed to the consequence that fewer mistakes reach customers, which leads to better service and less rework.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation for a small business of relying on a job interview as its only selection method.
items.canonical_answer: An interview is a conversation, so it tests what a candidate says rather than what they can do: a confident talker can present skills they do not have, which means the business may appoint on presentation rather than capability. Because a poor appointment only shows up weeks later, the business is likely to repeat the whole recruitment and selection process - new advertising, new interviews, more management time - so the limitation develops from weak evidence to a costly re-recruitment.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for interviews testing stated rather than demonstrated skill, developed because the small business has little other evidence to cross-check with, which leads to the consequence of repeating the process at full cost if the appointment fails.

items.prompt: Explain the features that separate the recruitment stage of employment from the selection stage.
items.canonical_answer: Recruitment and selection are two stages with distinct features. Recruitment identifies the vacancy and attracts suitable people to apply - its parts include the job description, the person specification and the advert, and its output is a pool of candidates. Selection chooses between the candidates who applied - what it includes is shortlisting, interviews, references and practical tests, and its output is one appointed person. The feature that separates them is direction: recruitment gathers candidates; selection reduces them.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - recruitment as gathering candidates with its documents and advert, selection as deciding with its shortlist, interviews and tests - and for what the pair includes in output terms: a pool of candidates against one appointment.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between internal recruitment and external recruitment.
items.canonical_answer: The boundary is whether the candidate already works for the business: internal recruitment fills a vacancy with an existing employee, advertised on a staff notice or internal vacancy list, whereas external recruitment reaches people outside the business through adverts, agencies or job sites. Both sides have consequences that follow from the boundary: internal is usually quicker and cheaper because the person is known, whereas external widens the candidate pool and can bring fresh outside ideas the business does not already hold.

items.canonical_answer: The features weighed are: the size of the candidate pool, because internal limits the choice to existing employees whereas external reaches anyone qualified; cost and speed, because internal needs no outside advertising and the person is already known, while external usually costs more and takes longer; knowledge of the business, which an internal candidate already has and an external one must be given; and fresh ideas, which external recruitment can bring and internal cannot. items.prompt: A lodge outside Outjo needs a new front-desk supervisor. Explain the stages the lodge should carry out from noticing the need to the new supervisor starting work.
items.canonical_answer: Given the vacancy, the stages run in order. First, identify the vacancy and draw up the documents: the job description states what the supervisor is responsible for, and the person specification states the skills and qualities needed. Second, advertise the vacancy internally and externally so candidates can apply. Third, receive the applications and shortlist against the specification, carrying the criteria forward. Fourth, interview and test the shortlist, with each candidate asked to handle a mock booking. Fifth, take up references to check what was claimed. Sixth, appoint the chosen candidate and agree the contract. The sequence is completed when the new supervisor is inducted into the role - which is the output the whole process exists to produce: an appointed, inducted employee rather than a pile of applications.
marking_guidance: Stages in order: award for the sequence - documents, advertise, shortlist, interview and test, references, appoint, induct. Input: award for starting from the given vacancy. items.prompt: Explain the difference between dismissal and redundancy, using an example of each.
items.canonical_answer: The boundary is where the cause sits: dismissal traces to the employee's own conduct or capability, whereas redundancy traces to the role itself disappearing. Example of dismissal: a warehouse assistant is dismissed for repeated lateness after two written warnings - the cause is conduct, and a fair dismissal needs a valid reason and a fair procedure. Example of redundancy: the same warehouse's second assistant job ends because a new scanning system removed the need for two people in that aisle - the person has done nothing wrong, and the law of unfair dismissal treats the two exits differently. Both sides of the contrast matter: conduct removed versus work removed.
marking_guidance: Both sides must appear: award for the boundary - conduct or capability against the role disappearing - with the contrast developed through one example of each, whereas a definition of one term alone is not a distinction.

items.prompt: Explain the features that keep redundancy, retirement and dismissal apart as three ways an employment ends.
items.canonical_answer: The three exits differ in cause and consequence. Redundancy: the features are a role the business no longer needs, compensation for the person, and no fault on their part. Retirement: the features are an agreed age or point at which working life ends, chosen rather than caused by the business. Dismissal: the features are a reason connected with the employee - conduct or capability - and a procedure of warnings before the exit. What keeps them apart is the cause: work removed, life stage reached, or behaviour ended the employment - and confusing them matters, because an employer who dresses a dismissal up as a redundancy is likely to face a claim of unfair dismissal.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of each exit - redundancy as work removed, retirement as an agreed life stage, dismissal as conduct or capability with warnings - and for what the comparison includes: the different cause of each.

items.prompt: Explain why a government places legal controls on employment, and why these controls also affect the businesses that employ.
items.canonical_answer:
The reason governments place these controls is to protect employees, because the two sides of employment are not equal in power: a written contract, protection from dismissal without a fair reason, equal treatment regardless of personal characteristics, safe conditions and a wage floor each exist to stop an employer using that power to pay too little, dismiss arbitrarily, choose staff on prejudice or leave the workplace unsafe - so employees work with security rather than fear.
The same controls affect the employer because compliance is a cost: wages at or above the legal minimum, safety equipment and training, and proper procedures before any dismissal all raise the cost of employing, and ignoring them risks penalties and claims. Businesses that respect the controls tend to gain trust and fewer disputes, though the details of the rules differ by country.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for protection of the weaker side of the employment relationship, because the purpose of each control is to stop a form of abuse. Second reason: award for the employer side - compliance raises costs, because the wage floor, safety spending and fair procedures are all expenses the business must plan for.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Nangolo Hardware is advertising for a new sales assistant on the radio, so this is part of its marketing to increase sales." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing advertising a job vacancy with advertising a product. Both use adverts, but they belong to different business functions. A job advert is part of recruitment: it is aimed at people who might want to work for the business, and it tells them the job, what the post requires and how to apply. A product advert is part of marketing: it is aimed at customers and tries to persuade them to buy. The test that tells them apart: ask what the listener is being asked to do. Nangolo Hardware's radio advert asks listeners to apply for the sales assistant post, so it is the advertising stage of recruitment. It is designed to attract suitable applicants, not buyers. Any extra sales it happened to bring would be a side effect; the business would judge the advert by the number and quality of the applications it attracts.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a vacancy advert is a stage of recruitment aimed at possible applicants, not a marketing advert aimed at customers.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Nakambale Plains Lodge used external recruitment when it sent its head chef on a two-week cookery course in Windhoek." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is confusing external recruitment with off-the-job training, which is sometimes called external training. External recruitment brings a new person into the business from outside - through a job advert, an employment agency or an online job site - to fill a vacancy. Off-the-job training develops someone who already works for the business by teaching them away from the workplace, for example at a college or training centre. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the business ends up with a new employee or with a better-skilled existing one. The lodge's head chef was employed before the course and is the same head chef afterwards; no vacancy was filled and nobody new joined the business. So the course is off-the-job training. It would have been external recruitment if the lodge had advertised the head chef's post outside the business and appointed someone new to it.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The job description for the bookkeeper at Okahandja Furniture Works says the applicant must hold an accounting certificate and have two years' experience." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing the job description with the person specification. A job description describes the job: its title, the duties and responsibilities it carries, and who the post-holder reports to - for this post, keeping the sales and purchase records and paying suppliers on time. A person specification describes the person wanted for the job: the skills, qualifications, experience and personal qualities a candidate needs. The job description is written first, and the person specification is written from it. The test that tells them apart: ask whether a line describes a task to be done or a quality the applicant must have. An accounting certificate and two years' experience are qualities of the applicant, so they belong in the person specification. The confusion matters because the two documents do different work in the process: the advert draws on the job description to tell applicants what the job involves, while shortlisting checks each application against the person specification.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a required qualification and experience describe the person wanted, so they belong in the person specification, not the job description.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Ndapewa works the packhouse's full 40-hour week at Kuiseb Fruit Packers, but just for the three months of the export season, so she is a part-time employee." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is confusing a part-time employee with a temporary one. Part-time describes hours: a part-time employee works fewer contracted hours each week than the business's full-time week. Temporary describes duration: a temporary employee is employed for a fixed period or a particular task, after which the contract ends. The two describe different things, so they vary independently - a worker can be full-time and temporary, or part-time and permanent. The test that tells them apart: ask which question the word answers - how many hours a week, or for how long. Ndapewa works the packhouse's full 40-hour week, so on hours she is full-time. Her contract lasts three months, so on duration she is temporary. She is a full-time temporary employee. Calling her part-time would also mislead the packhouse's planning, because it would count her as partial cover when she in fact provides a full working week for a limited period.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact a short contract makes an employee temporary, not part-time; part-time refers to working fewer than the full-time weekly hours.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Kalahari Print House made its receptionist redundant because she kept quoting customers the wrong prices after several warnings, and it has since advertised for a new receptionist." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is confusing dismissal with redundancy. Dismissal is when an employer ends an employee's contract because of the employee's own conduct or capability. Calling a dismissal a redundancy is likely to lead to a claim of unfair dismissal, because the two follow different procedures.

items.prompt: Tsumeb brickworks Kavio Bricks sold 40 per cent fewer bricks this year after a construction slowdown, and the board has announced that "the lazy ones will be dismissed first". The bagging line adds a second pressure: automation that does the loaders' work with fewer people, and a new training need - two operators must be trained. Recommendation: the board should run the reduction as redundancy, selecting against which skills the remaining work needs - retaining the kiln engineers and choosing production staff with aptitude to train as the bagging operators - rather than by cost or by personality. The counterargument is that redundancy costs compensation while dismissal does not, which is precisely why the board's instinct is tempting and wrong. The judgement depends on conditions: how far demand recovers, whether loaders can retrain as operators rather than being released, and applying the selection criteria fairly across the 30 workers.
